paper_core_claims.claim: Scientific hypotheses can be represented as programs in a domain-specific language whose primitives encode prior knowledge and constraints.
A neurosymbolic program combines a discrete symbolic architecture with continuous parameters/neural components and can be learned using symbolic, probabilistic and gradient methods.
Behavior analysis illustrates potential benefits and unresolved problems involving noisy/rare data, interpretable temporal programs, distribution shift and human domain knowledge.
Scaling requires discrete architecture search plus continuous optimization, while smooth semantics create an approximation/optimisability tradeoff.
Practical scientific deployment still lacks robust interpretability metrics, cross-domain benchmarks, reproducible stochastic search, accessible tools and scalable lifecycle integration.

function_concept_used_by_paper: A scientific function is framed as a hypothesis program in a domain-specific language. Its architecture composes symbolic control/higher-order primitives and domain concepts, while its components may carry differentiable parameters or neural modules. The paper also spans fully neural, neurosymbolic and fully symbolic cases, so function identity is a broad conceptual spectrum rather than one implemented contract or formal calculus.
representation_or_carrier: The principal carriers are DSL grammars, program architectures, numeric parameters, neural latent representations, symbolic primitives, expert constraints, informal theories/ethograms, examples and scientific data. The lifecycle diagram connects data curation, domain knowledge, model training, evaluation/interpretability and deployment. No machine-readable schema, artifact format or released registry instantiates this conceptual carrier stack.
specification_language: The paper proposes a DSL as the formal hypothesis space, with logical operations such as if, continuous-parametric functions, map/fold/map-prefix-style higher-order functions, domain features and constraints. Scientific inputs can also include examples, experimental context, ethograms, causal relations and natural-language knowledge. It does not define one concrete typed language, signature/precondition/effect schema, failure contract, permissions or a method that faithfully compiles all informal knowledge into a DSL.
compiler_or_generator: The surveyed NP pattern searches discrete program architectures and optimizes continuous parameters with gradient, probabilistic and symbolic techniques. NEAR, smooth interpretation, dPads, Houdini and library learning are cited exemplars. This paper contributes a synthesis and research agenda, not a new compiler, algorithm, implementation or execution trace; therefore its compiler evidence is architectural and secondary rather than an independently audited artifact.
interpreter_or_runtime: Discrete programs are interpreted with symbolic semantics, while smooth interpretation replaces discontinuities with differentiable approximations such as high-temperature hyperbolic-tangent or Gaussian smoothing. Neural modules and higher-order functions may execute inside the program. The paper explicitly warns that approximation alters semantics and creates a precision/trainability tradeoff; it defines no concrete runtime, effect policy, sandbox, trace format or semantic-preservation test.
composition_rule: Programs compose DSL functions, neural modules, algebraic primitives and higher-order operators through a discrete architecture; differentiable components compose by the chain rule. Library learning is proposed to mine recurring program patterns and add higher-level DSL primitives. No universal type/effect compatibility, rewrite equivalence, conflict resolution, dependency graph or safe cross-domain composition rule is specified.
state_or_effect_model: Scientific workflow state includes data curation, experimental context, domain knowledge, training, evaluation, interpretation and deployment. Behavior examples transform trajectories/pose features into classifications. These are workflow-level observations, not an operational effect system: external experiments, data mutation, interventions, permissions, causal side effects, transactions, compensation and rollback are not modeled.
uncertainty_model: The paper recognizes noisy/missing data, rare events, annotation ambiguity, distribution shift, stochastic program search and probabilistic methods. It suggests binomial behavior semantics and continuous relaxations as examples, and explicitly says stochastic search outputs may not be reproducible. It offers no calibrated uncertainty semantics, posterior/probability contract, confidence measure, experimental uncertainty analysis or quantitative reproducibility metric; indeed it states robust reproducibility metrics remain an open challenge.

equivalence_notions.boundary: Interpretability and manipulability do not prove the hypothesis true, causally correct or equivalent to the phenomenon.
The paper explicitly records approximation error; smooth and discrete programs are not semantically identical.
No quantitative metric, threshold or behavioral-equivalence test is defined.
No proof of substitutability, provenance preservation, regression safety or cross-domain meaning accompanies abstraction.

lifecycle_and_provenance: The paper explicitly depicts an iterative NP lifecycle from data curation and domain-knowledge encoding through model training, evaluation/interpretability and deployment, linked to the scientific process. It also advocates library learning and scientist feedback. This is useful lifecycle framing but not a registry: there are no immutable program IDs/hashes, source datasets, model/compiler versions, dependency/effect metadata, validation receipts, approvals, usage records, semantic versions, deprecation/tombstones, migrations or rollback. The mistaken historical S120-072 binding itself demonstrates why title, identifier, hash and provenance must be jointly validated.
limitations_and_failure_boundaries: The frozen registry binds the target title to unrelated arXiv:2211.05446; the correct latest paper is arXiv:2210.05050v2.
This is a perspective/workshop paper and research agenda, not a new algorithmic or controlled empirical contribution.
Examples and performance statements summarize cited prior work; they are not new results independently validated here.
No executable DSL, compiler, interpreter, library, dataset, model, benchmark or lifecycle artifact is released with the paper.
Scientific hypotheses as programs improve inspectability but do not establish truth, causal validity, correctness or safety.
DSL design itself requires experts, constrains expressivity and cannot tractably encode all informal/formal scientific knowledge.
Discrete architecture search is combinatorial/CPU-intensive and continuous optimization can be unstable.
Smooth interpretation changes semantics and trades output precision against optimization tractability.
Neurosymbolic programs may still be difficult for domain experts to interpret when primitives are generic or neural components dominate.
Behavior analysis is illustrative; generalization to high-dimensional video and other sciences is posed as open.
Noisy/missing data, rare classes, annotator ambiguity and distribution shift remain challenges rather than solved guarantees.
Stochastic synthesis may produce non-reproducible programs; no objective robust-reproducibility metric is supplied.
Compactness, completeness, stability, actionability and modularity are desiderata, not validated measurements in this paper.
Cross-domain benchmarks, expert evaluation panels and scientist-facing NP tools are proposed future work, not completed assets.
Workflow diagrams do not specify effects, experimental intervention safety, data governance, permissions, transactions or rollback.
Probabilistic examples do not define calibrated uncertainty or a general stochastic function semantics.
The model review and source-binding repair are not proof or independent empirical validation of cited NP systems.
what_the_paper_does_not_support: It does not prove that a synthesized scientific program is true, correct, causally valid or semantically equivalent to nature.
It does not introduce or empirically validate a new end-to-end NP system.
It does not establish scalable, stable, reproducible or cross-domain scientific discovery.
It does not supply a complete FunctionSpec/effect contract, versioned registry or provenance lifecycle.
It does not define calibrated probabilistic semantics for scientific functions.
It does not empirically validate ignition, Function OS deployment or neural-weight composition.

confirmed_projection: The paper gives strong conceptual support for treating scientific hypotheses as DSL programs that combine symbolic domain knowledge with neural/differentiable components, and it supplies a valuable lifecycle spanning data, knowledge, learning, evaluation and deployment. Support is partial because it is a perspective: no new compiler/runtime/artifact or evaluation is released, smooth semantics are approximate, effects and provenance are absent, and many desired properties are explicitly future challenges.
source_specific_reasoning: PARTIAL is required. The corrected latest v2 is a coherent, source-complete synthesis of FunctionSpec/Representation/Compiler/Interpreter/Composer/lifecycle ideas, and its candor about DSL design, scaling, approximation, interpretability and stochastic reproducibility is directly useful. But the paper does not implement or test an end-to-end system; all concrete achievements are citations; benchmarks/tools remain proposals; and the historical registry's unrelated PDF prevents the original extracted record from counting as evidence. The repaired exact paper supports architecture and gap framing, not proof or empirical confirmation of a complete Function OS.
